The {{nihongo| '''Katori Shrine'''|香取神宮|Katori Jingū}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} in the city of {{ill|Katori, Chiba|en|Katori, Chiba|qid=Q858357|lt=Katori|1=Katori, Chiba}} in {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|en|Chiba Prefecture|qid=Q80011|lt=Chiba Prefecture|1=Chiba Prefecture}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|qid=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former {{ill|Shimōsa Province|en|Shimōsa Province|qid=Q1053695|lt=Shimōsa Province|1=Shimōsa Province}}, and is the head shrine of the approximately 400 Katori shrines around the country (located primarily in the {{ill|Kantō region|en|Kantō region|qid=Q132480|lt=Kantō region|1=Kantō region}}).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}}</ref> The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 14, with a three-day Grand Festival held every 12 years.<ref>Plutschow. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. Page 173</ref>

==Enshrined ''kami''==
The primary ''[[kami]]'' of Katori Jingū is
* {{nihongo|[[Futsunushi|Futsunushi-no-kami]]|経津主神|}}, the ''kami'' of swords and lightning, and a general of [[Amaterasu]].

==History==
The foundation of Katori Jingū predates the historical period. Per the ''Hitachi-koku {{lang|ja-latn|[[Fudoki]]}}'', an ancient record and per shrine tradition, it was established in 643 BC, the 18th year of the reign of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|qid=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu|1=Emperor Jimmu}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.doshikai.org/bushido/articles/Katori_Shinto_Ryu.pdf |title=Katori Shinto Ryu |accessdate=2008-05-17 |work=The Doshikai}}</ref> During this period, the {{nihongo|{{ill|Ō clan|en|Ō clan|qid=Q11430816|lt=Ō clan|1=Ō clan}}|多氏|Ō-shi|}} migrated from {{ill|Higo Province|en|Higo Province|qid=Q259705|lt=Higo Province|1=Higo Province}} in [[Kyushu]], conquering local ''{{ill|Emishi|en|Emishi|qid=Q932574|lt=Emishi|1=Emishi}}'' tribes, and forming an alliance with the nearby Nakatomi clan, the progenitors of the [[Fujiwara clan]] at what is now [[Kashima Jingū|Kashima Jingū]]. As the ''Hitachi-koku Fudoki'' dates from the early 7th century, the shrine must certainly have been founded earlier than this. The shrine appears in all of the ''[[Rikkokushi]]'' official national histories, which cover events to 887. The shrine was regarded as a tutelary shrine of the Fujiwara clan, and a ''[[bunrei]]'' of [[Futsunushi]] was brought from Katori to be enshrined in the second sanctuary of [[Kasuga-taisha|Kasuga Taisha]] when that shrine was founded in {{ill|Nara (city)|en|Nara (city)|qid=Q169134|lt=Nara|1=Nara (city)}}.  In the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}} per the ''[[Engishiki]]'' (written in 927), Katori was listed as a {{nihongo|myōjin taisha|名神大|}} and was one of only three shrines (alongside [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingū]] and Kashima Jingū) to be given the higher-level designation of {{ill|List of Jingū|en|List of Jingū|qid=Q120680118|lt=''Jingū''|1=List of Jingū}}. In the Heian period, the shrine came to be regarded as the ''ichinomiya'' of the province.<ref name="Yoshiki">{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}}</ref>

During the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|qid=Q236205|lt=Kamakura|1=Kamakura period}} and {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|qid=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period|1=Muromachi period}}s, Katori Jingū was revered as a shrine for the {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|qid=Q38142|lt=military class|1=Samurai}} and received many donations from [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] and {{ill|Ashikaga Takauji|en|Ashikaga Takauji|qid=Q297107|lt=Ashikaga Takauji|1=Ashikaga Takauji}}. It also earned income from its control of fishing rights in the {{ill|Katori Sea|en|Katori Sea|qid=Q11667182|lt=Katori Sea|1=Katori Sea}} and highway barriers in both {{ill|Hitachi Province|en|Hitachi Province|qid=Q1055353|lt=Hitachi Province|1=Hitachi Province}} and Shimōsa. Under the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}} [[Tokugawa shogunate]], the shrine was rebuilt in 1607, and again in 1700. Many of the structures in the present shrine date from this 1700 rebuilding.<ref name="Yoshiki"/>

During the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}} era of {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|qid=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}}, the shrine was rated as a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 1st Rank |官幣大社|Kanpei Taisha}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]]<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125.</ref>
== History ==

=== Foundation ===
According to shrine tradition, the shrine was founded in the 18th year of Emperor Jimmu's reign. The details of its early history remain unclear, but the "Hitachi Province Fudoki" (compiled in the early 8th century) already mentions a branch shrine called "Katori Mikono Shrine," confirming its existence prior to that time.

Additionally, during ancient times, Katori Shrine, along with Kashima Shrine, served as a strategic base for the Yamato court's governance over the eastern provinces. Some theories suggest that the court's dedication of these shrines marked their founding. However, other theories propose the existence of pre-existing rituals that formed the foundation of the shrine's practices.

=== Overview of History ===
During the Nara period, Katori Shrine was deeply revered as a clan deity by the Fujiwara clan alongside Kashima Shrine. In 768, the Kasuga Shrine (present-day Kasuga Taisha) was established on Mount Mikasa in Nara as the Fujiwara clan's shrine. Deities were enshrined there from other locations: Takemikazuchi from Kashima (first hall), Futsunushi from Katori (second hall), Ame-no-Koyane from Hiraoka (third hall), and Himegami (fourth hall).

The shrine maintained a strong connection with the Fujiwara clan. In 777, it was promoted to the upper Rank of Senior Fourth Rank due to Fujiwara no Yoshitsugu's illness, where he revered it as his clan deity.

During the Heian period, the shrine received several Rank promotions:
- In 836, it was promoted from Junior Third Rank to Senior Second Rank.
- In 839, it received the Junior First Rank.
- In 882, it attained Senior First Rank with First Order of Merit.

In the "Engishiki" (927), Katori Shrine is listed under the Shimousa Province as "Katori Jingu" with the highest status as a Myōjin Taisha, receiving offerings during the monthly and harvest festivals. At that time, only Ise Jingu, Kashima Jingū, and Katori Jingu were designated with the title "Jingu."

During the medieval period, the shrine continued to be revered by samurai, including Minamoto no Yoritomo and Ashikaga Takauji. However, it also faced encroachments on its shrine lands by warrior families like the Chiba clan. The shrine controlled fishing communities and checkpoints in Hitachi and Shimousa provinces, securing significant income.

After the fall of the Chiba clan, Tokugawa Ieyasu granted the shrine 1,000 koku of red seal land in 1591. The Tokugawa shogunate continued its patronage, commissioning major reconstructions in 1607 and again in 1700. The current main hall, tower gate, and former worship hall (now prayer hall) date from the latter reconstruction.

In 1871, during the Meiji era, Katori Shrine was designated as a Kanpei Taisha under the modern shrine Ranking system. In 1942, it was recognized as an imperial shrine for state ceremonies. After World War II, it became a Beppyo Shrine under the Association of Shinto Shrines.

== Festivals ==
=== Shikinen Festival ===
[[File:Jinko Festival,Tsunomiya,Katori Jingu Shrine,Katori-city,Japan.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Shikinen Jinkosai (2014)}}]]
As a grand periodic festival, the '''Shikinen Jinkosai''' (式年神幸祭) is held once every 12 years during the [[Horse Year]]. While the regular Jinkosai is conducted annually on April 15th, the Shikinen Grand Festival takes place on both April 15th and 16th with large-scale events. Historically, it was also known as "Military God Festival" and "Military Encampment Festival."{{Sfn|香取軍神祭（国史）|1983}}

This festival is said to reenact the conquest of the eastern provinces by Futsunushi no Kami.{{Sfn|香取神宮（平凡社）|1996}} Originally named "Shikinen Sengu Grand Festival," it was conducted in conjunction with the periodic shrine rebuilding every 20 years.{{Sfn|香取小史|1995|p=26}} However, it declined around the time of the {{ill|Ōnin War|en|Ōnin War|qid=Q385676|lt=Ōnin War|1=Ōnin War}}, with the last occurrence in {{ill|1568|en|1568|qid=Q6648|lt=1568|1=1568}}, and was not revived until the Meiji era.{{Sfn|香取軍神祭（国史）|1983}} In Meiji 8 (1875), it was restored and held annually, but from Meiji 15 (1882), it was set to be conducted every Horse Year, continuing to the present day.{{Sfn|香取軍神祭（国史）|1983}}

The festival proceeds as follows:{{Sfn|香取小史|1995|p=26}}
* April 15: The Jinkosai procession, centered around the mikoshi (portable shrine), departs from the shrine and arrives at Tsunomiya. At the Tone River bank, the mikoshi is transferred to a ceremonial boat, and a ritual is performed onboard. This is followed by a welcoming ceremony by [[Kashima Jingū]]. After sailing upriver and landing at the Sawara river mouth, the procession stays overnight at the {{ill|Otabisho|en|Otabisho|qid=Q11489117|lt=Otabisho|1=Otabisho}}.
* April 16: The procession parades through the city and returns to the shrine by land.

== Festivals ==
=== Otaue Festival ===
[[File:Rice-transplanting Festival in Katori-jingu 1,katori-city,japan.jpg|thumb|180px|right|{{Center|{{ill|Otaue Festival|ja|御田植祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Otaue Festival|qq=}}}}]]
; {{ill|Otaue Festival|ja|御田植祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Otaue Festival|qq=}}
: The "Otaue-sai" is held on the first Saturday and Sunday of April. On the first day, the Cultivation Ritual (耕田式) is conducted, followed by the Rice Planting Ceremony (田植式) on the second day, both classified as Grand Festivals. Rice planting is performed in the shrine's sacred paddy field to pray for a bountiful harvest. Historical records mention it as early as the 2nd year of {{ill|Meitoku|en|Meitoku|qid=Q1145032|lt=Meitoku|1=Meitoku}} (1391), and it is counted among the "Three Great Otaue Festivals of Japan."<ref group="note">The "Three Great Otaue Festivals of Japan" include this festival at Katori Jingu, {{ill|Izawa-no-miya|en|Izawa-no-miya|qid=Q10885171|lt=Izawa-no-miya|1=Izawa-no-miya}} ({{ill|Shima, Mie|en|Shima, Mie|qid=Q338009|lt=Shima, Mie|1=Shima, Mie}}, {{ill|Isobe no Otaue|ja|磯部の御神田|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Isobe no Otaue|1=Isobe-no-Omita|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11588063}}), and {{ill|Sumiyoshi-taisha|en|Sumiyoshi-taisha|qid=Q705949|lt=Sumiyoshi Taisha|1=Sumiyoshi-taisha}} ({{ill|Osaka|en|Osaka|qid=Q35765|lt=Osaka|1=Osaka}}, {{ill|Sumiyoshi no Otaue|ja|住吉の御田植|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi no Otaue|1=Sumiyoshi-no-Otaue Festival|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11381803}}).</ref><ref name="Spring"/> For more details, see {{ill|Otaue Festival at Katori Jingu|ja|香取神宮御田植祭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Otaue Festival at Katori Jingu|1=Otaue Festival at Katori Jingū|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11667185}}.

; Reisai and Jinkosai
: Held on April 14th and 15th, both are Grand Festivals. The Reisai is the most important festival at the shrine. Since Katori Jingu is one of the {{ill|Chokusaisha|en|Chokusaisha|qid=Q175288|lt=Chokusaisha|1=Chokusaisha}}, an imperial envoy attends every six years (in the years of the Rat and the Horse).{{Sfn|香取小史|1995|p=25}} On the day following the Reisai, the Jinkosai is held, featuring a procession dressed in Heian period attire, with a ceremony conducted at the parking lot.<ref name="Spring">[http://www.katori-jingu.or.jp/siki_spring.htm Spring] (Official Website).</ref>

; Daikyōsai
: The "Daikyōsai" (大饗祭) takes place on January 30 and is classified as a Medium Festival. It is said to commemorate the deities Futsunushi no Kami and Takemikazuchi no Kami after their pacification of the land.{{Sfn|香取小史|1995|p=33}} The ceremony is held after sunset, featuring a variety of rare offerings presented before the deities.<ref>[http://www.katori-jingu.or.jp/siki_winter.htm Autumn] (Official Website).</ref>

; Danki-sai
: The "Danki-sai" (団碁祭) is held on December 7 and is considered a Medium Festival. Also known as the "Hachiseki Hattō Dango Festival" (八石八斗団子祭), it is a harvest thanksgiving ceremony where rice flour dumplings made from newly harvested grains are offered. Over 80 ring-shaped dumplings are dedicated to the shrine. Since sake is not offered, it is believed to be a festival to honor the goddess Himegami, who was responsible for the hospitality during the Daikyōsai.{{Sfn|香取小史|1995|p=35}}<ref>[http://www.kanko.chuo.chiba.jp/c_event/8164/ Danki-sai] (Chiba Prefecture Tourism Guide).</ref> After the ceremony, the dumplings are distributed to worshippers.

==Cultural Properties==
===National Treasures===
* {{nihongo|'''Kaijū Budō Kagami'''|海獣葡萄鏡|}},  {{ill|Tang dynasty|en|Tang dynasty|qid=Q9683|lt=Tang dynasty|1=Tang dynasty}} {{ill|China|en|China|qid=Q148|lt=China|1=China}}. This round {{ill|Cupronickel|en|Cupronickel|qid=Q649090|lt=Cupronickel|1=Cupronickel}} mirror has a diameter of 29.6 centimeters, and weight of 4.56 kilograms. It  is decorated with bas-relief flowers, insects and a variety of real and mythological animals. It is almost identical to a mirror held by the [[Shōsōin]] Treasury in {{ill|Nara (city)|en|Nara (city)|qid=Q169134|lt=Nara|1=Nara (city)}}. The mirror itself is preserved at the {{ill|Nara National Museum|en|Nara National Museum|qid=Q147312|lt=Nara National Museum|1=Nara National Museum}}. It was designated a {{ill|National Treasure (Japan)|en|National Treasure (Japan)|qid=Q1139795|lt=National Treasure|1=National Treasure (Japan)}} in 1953.<ref name="Bunka1">{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/381|title=海獣葡萄鏡|trans-title=Kaijū Budō Kagami|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |accessdate=August 20, 2020}}</ref>

===Important Cultural Properties ===
* ''[[Honden]]'', Edo period (1700).  The ''Honden'' of Katori Shrine was traditionally reconstructed every 20 years, similar to the system used at [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]] until the system fell apart during the {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|qid=Q204023|lt=Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}}. The current structure was built in 1700 and was designated as {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|qid=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property|1=Important Cultural Property (Japan)}} in 1977.<ref name="Bunka2">{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/469|title=香取神宮本殿|trans-title=Katori Jingū Hondenlanguage=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |accessdate=August 20, 2020}}</ref>
* ''{{ill|Rōmon|en|Rōmon|qid=Q3458957|lt=Rōmon|1=Rōmon}}'', Edo period (1700). The Rōmon gate of Katori Shrine was also constructed in 1700 and was designated an Important Cultural Property in 1983. It displays the shrine's name plaque written by [[:en:Fleet Admiral|Fleet Admiral]] [[Tōgō Heihachirō]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.katori-jingu.or.jp/houmotu.htm |script-title=ja:宝物・文化財 |accessdate=2008-05-17 |work=香取神宮 |language=Japanese |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090703080421/http://www.katori-jingu.or.jp/houmotu.htm |archivedate=2009-07-03 }}</ref><ref name="Bunka3">{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/470|title=香取神宮楼門|trans-title=Katori Jingū Rōmon =Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |accessdate=August 20, 2020}}</ref>
* {{nihongo|'''Koseto ōyū Kominu'''|古瀬戸黄釉狛犬|}}, {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|qid=Q236205|lt=Kamakura|1=Kamakura period}} to {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|qid=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period|1=Muromachi period}}.  The shrine has a ceramic [[:en:Setomono|Koseto]] pair of ''{{ill|Komainu|en|Komainu|qid=Q20155846|lt=Komainu|1=Komainu}},'' standing 17.6 and 17.9 centimeters high. One of these statues was featured on a 250 Yen {{ill|Definitive stamp|en|Definitive stamp|qid=Q1002873|lt=Definitive stamp|1=Definitive stamp}} of Japan. The set of statues was designated as an Important Cultural Property in 1953.<ref name="Bunka4">{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/5534|title=古瀬戸黄釉狛犬|trans-title=Koseto ōyū komainu =Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |accessdate=August 20, 2020}}</ref>
* {{nihongo|'''Sōryū kagami'''|双竜鏡|}}, {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}. This mirror has a diameter 20.5&nbsp;cm and is made of white copper. It is inscribed with the date of 1149, and is the oldest example of an inscribed Japanese mirror. The style is different from general Japanese mirrors, and was influenced by {{ill|Song dynasty|en|Song dynasty|qid=Q7462|lt=Song dynasty|1=Song dynasty}} China or {{ill|Goryeo|en|Goryeo|qid=Q28208|lt=Goryeo|1=Goryeo}}. It was designated on November 14, 1953.<ref name="Bunka5">{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/5552|title=双竜鏡|trans-title=Sōryū kagami =Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |accessdate=August 20, 2020}}</ref>
* {{nihongo|'''Katori ōnegike monjo'''|香取大禰宜家文書 |}}, {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian|1=Heian period}} to {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}. This is a set of 381 documents that was in the possession of the Katori clan, the hereditary priesthood of the shrine. It was collectively designated on November 14, 1953.<ref name="Bunka7">{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/101/00001492|title=香雲閣|trans-title=Kaun-kaku =Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |accessdate=August 20, 2020}}</ref>

===Registered Tangible Cultural Properties===
* {{nihongo|'''Kaun-kaku'''|香雲閣 |}}, {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}}. This two-story, hipped-roof Japanese-style building is located on the southeast side of the Katori Jingu Shrine and has been used for meetings. It was designated in 2000.<ref name="Bunka7"/>
* {{nihongo|'''[[Haiden (Shinto)|haiden]]'''|香雲閣 |}}, [[:en:Showa period|Showa period]]. This building was constructed during a major renovation from 1945 by the Shrine Bureau of the Ministry of Home Affairs. It was designated in 2001.<ref name="Bunka8">{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/101/00002134|title=香取神宮拝殿・幣殿・神饌所|trans-title=Katori Jingu Shrine, Heiden, Shinsensho =Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |accessdate=August 20, 2020}}</ref>

'''Katori Jingu''' (香取神宮, pronounced “Katori Jingu”) is a Shinto shrine located in Katori, Chiba Prefecture. It is designated as a Shikinaisha (Meishindaisya) and is the ichinomiya of Shimousa Province. Under the former Modern Shrine Ranking System it was classified as a Kanpei Taisha; today it is recognized as a Betsuhyo Shrine under the Association of Shinto Shrines.
== Overview ==
Located atop a hill known locally as "Kamegase-yama" (“Tortoise Shell Mountain”) on the right bank of the lower Tone River in northeastern Chiba Prefecture, Katori Jingu stands on a gently elevated plateau. In Japanese mythology, during the subjugation of the land by Ōkuninushi (in the episode known as the transfer of the country from Ōkuninushi), the deity [[Keizutsushi Ōkami|Keizutsushi Ōkami]] (also read “Futsunushi”) was celebrated for his valor. This makes the shrine one of the most venerable ancient shrines in the nation.

Historically, the shrine was esteemed by the imperial court as a divine force in the subjugation of the Emishi, and later as the tutelary (ujigami) shrine of the Fujiwara clan. Its martial potency continued to be recognized from the medieval period onward, and successive warrior regimes revered it as a war god. Even today, Katori Jingu is deeply respected in martial arts circles.

In terms of cultural properties, the shrine houses a bronze mirror with grapevine motifs (known as the Kaijū Budōkyō) dating from the Tang dynasty—which is designated as a National Treasure. Among its buildings, the main hall and the roof gate (from the Edo period), as well as artifacts such as a mirror from the Heian period and ancient guardian dog statues (komainu) from medieval times, have been designated as Important Cultural Properties. Many other cultural treasures have been preserved to the present day.
== Enshrined Deity ==
The primary deity enshrined at Katori Jingu is a single kami:<ref group="Note">The official records (including the "Goyuisyo" on the shrine’s website and the "Shinshū Katori Jingu Shoshi") state that only one deity is enshrined. However, some texts (e.g. {{Harvnb|Katori Jingu (Heibonsha)|1996}}) mention that in some secondary halls three deities appear: Takemikazuchi Ōkami, Amanokoyane no Mikoto, and a female deity.</ref>
* '''[[Keizutsushi Ōkami|Keizutsushi Ōkami]]''' (read “Futsunushi no Ōkami”)
** He is also known by the alternative names “Iwahinushi no Kami” (or “Saishu no Kami”) and “Saijin Ototo” in various sources.

=== About the Enshrined Deity ===
As indicated, the principal deity of Katori Jingu is known as Keizutsushi (or Futsunushi). Regarding his origins, one account in the ''Nihon Shoki'' (circa 720 AD) presents an alternate tradition: when [[Izanagi]] slew [[Kagu-tsuchi|Kagutsuchi]] (the fire god), the blood that dripped from his severed head solidified into a mass of rocks which became the progenitor of Futsunushi.<ref group="Primary Source" name="Shinodai">''Nihon Shoki'', Kamiyo section.</ref> Another version relates that the blood staining the rock produced deities named Iwasaku and Nesaku, whose offspring, Iwatsutsuno-o and Iwatsutsuno-me, later became the parents of Futsunushi.<ref group="Primary Source" name="Shinodai2">''Nihon Shoki'', another section.</ref> Later, in the "corrected" account of the ''Nihon Shoki'', it is recorded that prior to the descent of the heavenly grandchild, Futsunushi, together with [[Takemikazuchi Ōkami|Takemikazuchi]] (the deity of Kashima Jingū), was dispatched to Izumo to negotiate with Ōkuninushi over the transfer of the land. (It is notable that Futsunushi does not appear in the ''Kojiki''.)

Concerning the relationship between Katori and Kashima, the ''Nihon Shoki'' contains a passage stating that “the deity (Saishu) now resides in the land of Katori,” with “Katori” being derived from the ancient word for “oar” (suggesting “paddle” or “taking the oar”). Furthermore, the ''Kogo Shūi'' (compiled in 807 AD)<ref group="Primary Source">''Kogo Shūi'' (see also the {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}).</ref> states that “Futsunushi no Kami is enshrined in Katori of Shimousa Province.” In the "Chigasai" of the ''Engishiki'' (compiled in 927 AD)<ref group="Primary Source">''Engishiki'', Volume 8, section on Chigasai (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}).</ref> the deity is described as “sitting as Iwahinushi no Kami in Katori.”

The nature of the deity is understood primarily from the myth that recounts his role in subjugating the land, and he is regarded as a war and martial god. The term “Futsu” in his name is thought to be evocative of the divine sword [[Futsunomitama]], symbolizing the sharpness of blades.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (National History)|1983}}</ref> As evidence of his martial aspect, a poem in the late Heian period text ''Ryōjin Hishō'' refers to “the war god of the east—from Seki, namely Kashima, Katori, and Suwa.”<ref group="Primary Source">{{sfn|Katori Jingu (National History)|1983}}</ref> Alternatively, based on the ancient name “Kajitori” (meaning “one who takes an oar”), some view the deity as originally having been worshipped as a god of navigation. There remain various theories regarding the shrine’s founding and the origin of its enshrinement (see the “Research” section below).
== Features ==
[[File:Kashima-jingu roumon.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Kashima Jingū (located in Kashima, Ibaraki Prefecture, the ichinomiya of Hitachi Province). It has a deep historical connection with Katori Jingu, and the two are traditionally mentioned together.}}]]
Katori Jingu is closely related to [[Kashima Jingū]] (located in Kashima, Ibaraki Prefecture, the ichinomiya of Hitachi Province, see coordinates {{Coord|35|58|07.88|N|140|37|53.37|E|region:JP-08_type:landmark|name=Hitachi Ichinomiya: Kashima Jingū}}). Traditionally, the two shrines have been paired and referred to collectively as “Kashima–Katori.”

Both shrines have long been venerated by the imperial court. This deep veneration is attributed to the fact that both have been worshipped as deities of war.

In ancient eastern Kantō, an inland sea known as the {{ill|Katori Sea|en|Katori Sea|qid=Q11667182|lt=Katori Sea|1=Katori Sea}} spanned an area that included present-day {{ill|Kasumigaura|en|Kasumigaura|qid=Q353440|lt=Kasumigaura|1=Kasumigaura}} (Kitauura and Nishiura), [[Imba-numa]], and [[Tegama-numa]]. Both shrines were strategically located at the gateway to this inland sea, which functioned as a transportation hub for the Yamato regime’s military expeditions against the Emishi.<ref name="Q5">{{ill|Yamamoto Hirofumi|ja|山本博文|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamamoto Hirofumi|1=Hirofumi Yamamoto|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11468918}}, “The History You Do Not Know of Chiba Prefecture” (Yōsen-sha) Q5 (pp. 26–27).</ref>

Examples of imperial attention include:
* **Divine District (Shingun):** At both Kashima Jingū and Katori Jingu, the respective districts (Kashima District in Hitachi and Katori District in Shimousa) were designated as sacred territories (Shingun), meaning the entire district was considered under the shrine’s divine protection.<ref>{{sfn|Okada|2011}}</ref> Such arrangements were rare and always located in areas of strategic military and transport significance.
* **Imperial Envoys (Kashima/Katori Tsukai):** Both shrines annually received envoys (Chokushi) from the imperial court – sometimes separately as Kashima Tsukai and Katori Tsukai, or collectively as “Kashima Katori Tsukai.” Outside of the Ise and Kinai regions, regular envoy dispatches are seen only at Kashima and, every six years, at Kasuga Jingu, making the annual dispatches to these shrines extremely unusual.<ref>{{sfn|Okada|2011}}</ref>
* **Use of the Title “Jingū”:** In the ''Engishiki Jinmyōchō'' (a Heian period list of state shrines), the title “Jingū” was applied only to three shrines: Ise Jingu (the Inner Shrine of Ise), Kashima Jingū, and Katori Jingu.<ref group="Note">Prior to the Heian period, the title “Jingū” appears in texts like the ''Kojiki'' and ''Nihon Shoki'' (for example, at Ishigami Jingu), but in the ''Engishiki Jinmyōchō'' it is recorded as “Ishigami Zaburumi-no-Mitama Jinja.” {{Harvnb|Okada|2011}}</ref>

Katori Jingu also enjoyed strong veneration from the Fujiwara clan. When Kasuga Jingu in Nara (established as the tutelary shrine of the Fujiwara) was founded, the deity of Kashima Jingū was enshrined in the first hall, while the deity of Katori Jingu was enshrined in the second, and the ancestral deity of the Fujiwara, [[Amanokoyane no Mikoto|Amanokoyane no Mikoto]], was enshrined in the third hall—placing Katori Jingu’s deity above Amanokoyane.<ref>See Inagaki Eizō, “Kasuga Jingu” in the National History Encyclopedia, Yoshikawa Kōbunkan.</ref> In the medieval period, even as the warrior class came to dominate, both shrines continued to be venerated as deities of war. Today, they are still strongly revered within martial arts circles; many dojos display paired hanging scrolls inscribed “Great Deity of Kashima” and “Great Deity of Katori.”
== History ==

=== Founding ===
According to shrine tradition, Katori Jingu was founded in the 18th year of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|qid=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu|1=Emperor Jimmu}}’s reign. Although details of its early establishment remain unclear, the ''Hitachi Fudoki'' (compiled in the early 8th century)<ref group="Primary Source" name="Yukue">''Hitachi Fudoki'', Yukue-gun section (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}).</ref> already mentions a branch shrine known as “Katori Shinshiro,” indicating that the original worship had been established well before that time.

Furthermore, because Katori Jingu (along with Kashima Jingū) served as a base for the Yamato regime’s expansion in eastern provinces, some scholars argue that its founding was an act of the imperial court establishing administrative centers in the region.<ref name="Katori Heritage"/>

=== Historical Overview ===
[[File:Kasuga-taisha11bs3200.jpg|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Kasuga Jingu (Nara Prefecture, Nara City)}}{{Small|When Kasuga Jingu was founded as the tutelary shrine of the Fujiwara clan, Keizutsushi was enshrined in its second hall while Kashima’s deity occupied the first hall.}}]]
During the Nara period, the Katori shrine was venerated as a tutelary (ujigami) shrine by the Fujiwara clan, along with Kashima Jingū. In the 2nd year of the {{ill|Jingo-keiun|en|Jingo-keiun|qid=Q1373049|lt=Shingō|1=Jingo-keiun}} era (768 AD), a shrine (later known as Kasuga Jingu) was established on Mount Migamine in Nara as the tutelary shrine of the Fujiwara clan; during this founding, the deities from Kashima Jingū (in the first hall), Katori Jingu (in the second hall), and from Hiraoka (in the third hall) were enshrined.<ref group="Note">The precise date of Kasuga Jingu’s founding is unclear; the “Shingō 2” date is based on the shrine’s records and is corroborated by an entry in the ''Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku'' dated August 26 of Genkei 8.</ref> The close relationship with the Fujiwara clan is further attested by the fact that in the 8th year of the {{ill|Hōki|en|Hōki|qid=Q18520676|lt=Hōki|1=Hōki}} era (777 AD), during the illness of Fujiwara no Yoshitsugu, the deity of Katori Jingu was conferred a court Rank of Senior Fourth.<ref group="Primary Source" name="Hōki8">{{sfn|Katori Jingu (National History)|1983}}</ref>

In the Heian period, the deity’s court Rank is recorded as follows: in the 3rd year of the {{ill|Jōwa|en|Jōwa|qid=Q3577279|lt=Shōwa|1=Jōwa}} era (836 AD) he was awarded Senior Second; in the 6th year of Shōwa (839 AD) he was promoted to Junior First; and in the 6th year of the {{ill|Gangyō|en|Gangyō|qid=Q747451|lt=Genkei|1=Gangyō}} era (882 AD) he appears to have been conferred Senior First, First Class Merit.<ref group="Primary Source" name="Genkei6">{{sfn|Katori Jingu (National History)|1983}}</ref>

The ''Engishiki Jinmyōchō'' (compiled in 927 AD) lists the shrine in the Katori District of Shimousa Province as “Katori Jingu, Meishindaisya, Tsukiji Shin-Narate,” and records that during the Tsukiji Festival and the New Rice Festival offerings such as cloth were made. Notably, in this document the title “Jingū” is used only for Ise Jingu, Kashima Jingū, and Katori Jingu. In Shimousa Province, Katori Jingu came to be regarded as the ichinomiya (primary shrine) and was venerated throughout the province.<ref group="Note">Although the term “ichinomiya” does not appear in early documents, its later usage is well attested. {{Harvnb|Ichinomiya System|2000|p=218}}</ref>

During the medieval period, as the era of the warrior class began, the martial character of the deity was maintained and the shrine was venerated as a war god by military leaders such as Minamoto no Yoritomo and Ashikaga Takauji.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Kakudō)|1984}}</ref> However, during this time there were also frequent encroachments upon the shrine’s territory by local samurai clans like the Chiba, leading to numerous legal disputes.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Heibonsha)|1996}}</ref> Additionally, starting in the medieval period, special revenue was derived from offerings collected from those engaged in fishing activities on the Katori Sea.

After the fall of the Chiba clan, control of the region passed to Tokugawa Ieyasu. In the 19th year of the {{ill|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|en|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|qid=Q1145058|lt=Tenshō Era|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)}} era (1591 AD), a cadastral survey was conducted which drastically reduced the shrine’s domain, granting it 1,000 koku as revenue land (朱印地). Records from the Genroku period indicate that the shrine’s domain comprised 900 koku for the main shrine, 100 koku for the subsidiary shrine, and 20 koku for the associated temple.<ref>{{sfn|Shrine Domain (National History)|1983}}</ref>

* In the history of the Six Provinces, records of the bestowal of divine Ranks include:
** In the 8th year of the {{ill|Hōki|en|Hōki|qid=Q18520676|lt=Hōki|1=Hōki}} era (777 AD), on July 16, a decree awarded the Kashima deity a Rank of Senior Fourth (as recorded in the ''Shoku Nihon Kōki'') – the inscription reads “Katori Jingu.”
** In the 3rd year of the {{ill|Jōwa|en|Jōwa|qid=Q3577279|lt=Shōwa|1=Jōwa}} era (836 AD), on May 9, a decree elevated the Rank from Junior Third to Senior Second – the inscription reads “Iwahinushi no Kami.”
** In the 6th year of Shōwa (839 AD), on October 29, a decree conferred the Rank of Junior First – the inscription reads “Iwahinushi no Kami.”
** In the 6th year of the {{ill|Gangyō|en|Gangyō|qid=Q747451|lt=Genkei|1=Gangyō}} era (882 AD), on December 9, a decree granted Senior First, First Class Merit – the inscription reads “Katori Jingu.”
* As a reference, regarding the Rank conferred on the Kasuga deity (of [[Kasuga Jingu]]) for “Iwahinushi no Kami Daibito”:
** In the 3rd year of the {{ill|Kashō|en|Kashō|qid=Q1373157|lt=Kashō|1=Kashō}} era (850 AD), on September 15, he was awarded Senior First (as recorded in the ''Nihon Buntoku Tennō Jitsuroku'').<ref group="Primary Source" name="Kashō3">{{sfn|Katori Jingu (National History)|1983}}</ref>
** {{Small|Note: In that account, three other deities of Kasuga are also Ranked; the fact that both the original shrine and Kasuga Jingu received these Ranks concurrently suggests a simultaneous conferment.<ref name="Kasuga Heibonsha">{{sfn|Katori Jingu (National History)|1983}}</ref>}}
=== Shrine Officials ===
==== Administrative Structure ====
According to the ''Engishiki'' (established in the 5th year of the {{ill|Tenshō|ja|延長|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshō|1=Enchō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q97379316}} era, 927 AD)<ref group="Primary Source">''Engishiki'', Volume 15, section on the internal administrative rules for Katori and Kashima (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}).</ref><ref group="Primary Source">''Engishiki'', Volume 3, section on temporary festival attire for Katori (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}).</ref><ref group="Primary Source">''Engishiki'', Volume 3, section on the court Rank for the shrine head (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}).</ref> the administrative structure consisted of one head priest (daiguji), one assistant priest (one-negi), two ceremonial ritual officials (monoomi), six musicians, and eight dancers. The head priest was regarded as equivalent in Rank to Junior Eighth.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Heibonsha)|1996}}</ref>

From the late Heian period through the medieval period, records indicate that the number of priests increased to well over one hundred, including positions such as the chief priest, head assistant priest, deputy celebrants, ritual officials, and various other ceremonial roles.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Heibonsha)|1996}}</ref>

==== Ritual Clan ====
Tradition holds that the original ritual clan of the shrine was the “Katori-ujī” (Katori clan).<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Kakudō)|1984}}</ref> According to the “Katori Daiguji Keizu” (genealogical record of the head priest of Katori Jingu), the progenitor was Nae Mase no Mikoto (also known as Amanonamae no Mikoto), a son of Futsunushi, and during the reign of Emperor Bidatsu (circa 572–585 AD) his descendant Toyosato began using the name “Katori-ujī” and, from the reign of Emperor Bunmu (circa 697–707 AD), started serving at the Katori shrine.<ref>Excerpt from ''Zoku Gunsho Ruiju'', Volume 7 (lower section).</ref>

Thus, the Katori clan claimed descent from Futsunushi; however,<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu Shoshi|1995|p=47}}</ref> later genealogies record that a branch of the [[Ōnakata Nakatomi Clan]] came to control the head priest position, with Ōnakata Kiyoshige (from the Nakatomi clan) assuming the role of daiguji and his son Akio taking over as one-negi. (The reliability of these names and dates is subject to debate.)<ref>{{sfn|Matsuo|2014|pp=260–265}}</ref> Thereafter, until the end of the Heian period, both the daiguji and one-negi positions were monopolized by the Nakatomi clan.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Kakudō)|1984}}</ref> However, because Katori Jingu served as the tutelary shrine of the Fujiwara clan, the appointment of its officials was managed centrally by the Fujiwara.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Heibonsha)|1996}}</ref>

In the 1st year of the [[:en:Kōchi|Kōchi]] era (1142 AD), an appointment from the Kashima Jingū’s Nakatomi clan to the head priest position at Katori Jingu was recorded; thereafter, a rivalry emerged between the Nakatomi factions of Kashima and Katori over the daiguji post.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Heibonsha)|1996}}</ref> Both sides lobbied with the Kamakura Shogunate and the regents, and by the [[Kankei]] era (circa 1229–1232 AD) the Nakatomi faction associated with Kashima prevailed.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Heibonsha)|1996}}</ref>

Following this, the influence of the Fujiwara waned, and internal conflicts within the Nakatomi clan over the daiguji, one-negi, and shrine domain ensued.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Heibonsha)|1996}}</ref> These disputes continued until around the 7th year of the {{ill|Ōan|en|Ōan|qid=Q1146245|lt=Ōan|1=Ōan}} era (circa 1374 AD), after which the branch of the one-negi family consolidated power and the situation stabilized during the late Kamakura to Muromachi periods. Later, although the shrine came under the control of the Tokugawa Shogunate in modern times, periodic conflicts still recurred.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Heibonsha)|1996}}</ref>

=== Shrine Domain ===
According to the ''Engishiki''<ref name="ShikibuUpper" group="Primary Source">''Engishiki'', Volume 18, section on district officials (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}).</ref>, the region in which the shrine is located in Shimousa Province (the Katori District) was designated as a divine district (Shingun)—meaning the entire district was under the shrine’s sacred jurisdiction. The ''Hitachi Fudoki''<ref group="Primary Source">''Hitachi Fudoki'', Kashima-gun section.</ref> records that Kashima District (also known as Kashima-gun in Hitachi, corresponding to Katori District) was established as a divine district in the 5th year of the Taika era (649 AD), suggesting that Katori District was established in a similar manner.<ref>{{sfn|Katori District (Heibonsha)|1996}}</ref><ref>{{sfn|Katori District (Kakudō)|1984}}</ref>

In the 1st year of the {{ill|Daidō|en|Daidō|qid=Q1373191|lt=Daidō|1=Daidō}} era (806 AD)<ref group="Primary Source">''Shinshō Kakutoku Shō'', Volume 10 (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}).</ref>, it is recorded that the shrine controlled 70 household registers (fūdō).<ref>{{sfn|Shrine Domain (National History)|1983}}</ref> By the 11th century, there are records of donations of household registers from the Fujiwara clan.<ref>{{sfn|Shrine Domain (National History)|1983}}</ref>

During the medieval period, disputes among the shrine officials and encroachments on the shrine’s domain by local warrior clans (such as the Chiba) led to frequent lawsuits.<ref>{{sfn|Shrine Domain (National History)|1983}}</ref> In addition, from the medieval period onward, a special revenue called “Kaifu”—from offerings collected from fishermen working in the Katori Sea—became an important income source.

After the fall of the Chiba clan, under Tokugawa Ieyasu’s rule in the Kantō region, a cadastral survey was conducted in the 19th year of the [[:en:Tenshō|Tenshō]] era (1591 AD)<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Heibonsha)|1996}}</ref>, which resulted in a drastic reduction of the shrine’s domain. That same year, 1,000 koku were granted as revenue land (朱印地). Later records from the Genroku period indicate that the shrine’s domain amounted to 900 koku for the main shrine, 100 koku for the subsidiary shrine, and 20 koku for the associated temple.<ref>{{sfn|Shrine Domain (National History)|1983}}</ref>

=== Shrine Construction ===
According to the ''Nihon Kōki''<ref group="Primary Source">''Nihon Kōki'', Kōnin 3 (812 AD, June 5; see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}).</ref>, the rebuilding of Katori Jingu is attested. Later texts such as the ''Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku''<ref group="Primary Source" name="Genkei6">{{sfn|Katori Jingu (National History)|1983}}</ref> and the ''Engishiki''<ref group="Primary Source">''Engishiki'', Volume 3, section on temporary festival and shrine repair (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}).</ref> state that even before 812 AD, Katori Jingu had instituted a Shikinen Sengu (periodic rebuilding) every 20 years.

Records of reconstruction during the late Heian period include, for example, the 3rd year of Hōen (1137 AD), the 2nd year of Kyūsu (1155 AD), the 1st year of Jishō (1177 AD), the 4th year of Kenkyū (1193 AD, delayed due to a great wind), the 8th year of Kenkyū (1197 AD), the 1st year of Jōkyū (1219 AD; delayed due to warfare and postponed to the 3rd year of Karoku in 1227 AD), the 3rd year of Hōji (1249 AD), the 8th year of Bun'ei (1271 AD), the 5th year of Shōō (1292 AD), the 2nd year of Gendoku (1330 AD), during the Jōji period (1362–1367 AD), the 2nd year of Shitoku (1385 AD), the 5th year of Ōe (1398 AD), the 2nd year of Eikyō (1430 AD), and the 2nd year of Kyōroku (circa 1529 AD), as recorded in various sources.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Kakudō)|1984}}</ref> Other sources also indicate rebuilding in years such as the 5th year of Shōwa (1316 AD), the 31st year of Ōe (1424 AD), the 15th year of Bunmei (1483 AD), and the 1st year of Meiō (1492 AD).<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Kakudō)|1984}}</ref> In the Kamakura period, the rebuilding was observed approximately every 20 years, but after the Nanboku-chō period this practice became difficult to maintain and few records survive.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Kakudō)|1984}}</ref>

During the Edo period, a major reconstruction was carried out in the 12th year of the {{ill|Keichō|en|Keichō|qid=Q1328185|lt=Keichō|1=Keichō}} era (1607 AD)<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Kakudō)|1984}}</ref>. Then, in the 13th year of the Genroku era (1700 AD), another reconstruction was undertaken; the present main hall and roof gate date from this Genroku period rebuilding.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Kakudō)|1984}}</ref>

On May 14 of the 4th year of the Meiji era (1871 AD), Katori Jingu was designated as a {{ill|Kanpei Taisha|en|Kanpei Taisha|qid=Q134917279|lt=Kanpei Taisha|1=Kanpei Taisha}} under the Modern Shrine Ranking System,<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=69}}</ref> and in 1942 (Showa 17) it was reclassified as a [[Chokusaisha]]. In the postwar period, it is now categorized as a [[Betsuhyo Shrine]] under the Association of Shinto Shrines.

== Shrine Complex ==
The hill upon which the shrine is enshrined is called “Kamegase-yama” (“Tortoise Shell Mountain”) because of its shape—low in the center and higher around the edges.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=50}}</ref>

Because the shrine grounds are considered a sacred precinct and remain largely untouched, many ancient cedar trees (sugi) and other large trees such as Inumaki, momi, and black pines grow here.<ref name="Fusa"/> Not only does the site contain an upper canopy layer, but it also supports sub-canopy, shrub, and forest floor vegetation. The ancient cedar forest is one of the most prominent in the prefecture and has been designated a Natural Monument by Chiba Prefecture.<ref name="Fusa"/>

=== Shrine Buildings ===
[[File:Katori-jingu honden.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Main Hall (Registered as a National Important Cultural Property)}}{{Small|Viewed from the northeast; the rear is the worship hall.}}]]
[[File:Katori-jingu romon.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Roof Gate (Registered as a National Important Cultural Property)}}]]
[[File:Katori-jingu kyuhaiden.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Prayer Hall (Former Worship Hall; designated as a Chiba Prefecture Cultural Property)}}]]
The principal shrine buildings currently in use were built in the 13th year of the Genroku era (1700 AD) under the orders of Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, the 5th shogun of the Edo Shogunate. At that time, the main hall, worship hall, and roof gate were constructed; the worship hall was later rebuilt between 1936 (Showa 11) and 1940 (Showa 15) and is now used as the Prayer Hall. During the Showa major restoration, an offering hall and a sacred kitchen were also built. The main shrine buildings (the main hall, offering hall, and worship hall) are arranged in the Gongen-zukuri style, meaning they form a continuous complex.
The '''Main Hall''' was constructed in Genroku 13 (1700 AD) in the Nagare-zukuri style with three bays and a cypress-bark roof, facing south. It is one of the largest structures of its type.<ref name="Fusa"/> Its eaves are incorporated into the interior, and it has a short eave at the rear.<ref name="Fusa"/> Although officially described as “Nagare-zukuri,” the presence of the rear eave has led some scholars to consider it a variant of “Ryū-zukuri.” The walls and pillars are finished in black lacquer, giving it a striking dark appearance. The roof is currently cypress bark, although it is said that it was once roofed with persimmon bark.<ref name="Fusa">[http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/pbbunkazai/  Chiba Prefecture Cultural Property Navigation] (Chiba Prefectural Board of Education)</ref> Its design is characteristic of the early modern period, with elements of the Momoyama style as well as techniques from the Keichō period.<ref name="Fusa"/> Extensive repairs were made to the main hall during the Showa restoration.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Heibonsha)|1996}}</ref> It is believed that the current main hall follows the tradition of an earlier building known as the “Asame-dono,” which once served as a temporary hall during Shikinen Sengu (periodic rebuilding). Due to its unusual configuration—where the sacred seat within the hall is set back toward the rear eave rather than directly facing the entrance—this structure is considered exceptional.<ref>{{sfn|Miura|1986}}</ref>
The Worship Hall (Haiden), Offering Hall (Heiden), and Sacred Kitchen (Shinsen-sho) were constructed during the Showa restoration. These are single-storied wooden structures with cypress bark roofs.<ref name="National Property">[http://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/bsys/index.asp National Cultural Properties Database]</ref> They adjoin the main hall in a continuous row in the Gongen-zukuri style.<ref name="Fusa"/> In addition, the Worship Hall’s front is decorated with a “Chidori-hafu” design.<ref name="Fusa"/> The former worship hall (old Haiden) was originally finished in red lacquer but was redesigned during the restoration with a black lacquer core and vivid decorative details to match the main hall.<ref name="Fusa"/>
The '''Roof Gate''' was built in Genroku 13 (1700 AD) as a three-bay, one-door structure in the irimoya style. Its roof is now covered with copper plates, though it was originally roofed with cypress bark (now called “Kokerabuki”).<ref name="Treasures">[http://www.katori-jingu.or.jp/houmotu.htm Treasures and Cultural Properties] (Official Website)</ref> Its style is purely Japanese, with walls and pillars finished in red lacquer. Within the gate, statues commonly known as the “Left Minister and Right Minister” are enshrined—the right figure is traditionally identified as [[Takeuchi no Sukune]], and the left as {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en|Fujiwara no Kamatari|qid=Q433995|lt=Fujiwara no Kamatari|1=Fujiwara no Kamatari}}.<ref name="Treasures"/> The horizontal scroll on the upper part of the gate is by [[Tōgō Heihachirō]]. The Roof Gate has become an iconic symbol of the shrine.<ref name="Treasures"/>
The '''Prayer Hall''' (formerly the old Haiden) was originally built as the worship hall in Genroku 13 (1700 AD) but was relocated to the southeast during the Showa restoration and then shifted approximately 1.5 meters further west in Showa 59 (1984 AD).<ref name="Fusa"/> It is five bays wide and three bays deep, constructed in the irimoya style.<ref name="Fusa"/> Its roof is now copper-plated, though it was originally cypress bark and was replaced in Showa 40 (1965 AD). The walls and pillars are finished in red lacquer. The former worship hall is one of the more substantial structures and clearly displays design elements characteristic of its construction period.<ref name="Fusa"/>
In addition, the shrine’s treasury (Shinko) was built in 1909 (Meiji 42) in wooden Kōkurō-zukuri style (designated as a Katori City Cultural Property). The Shintokukan, built in 1961 (Showa 36) on the former site of the head priest’s residence, uses a gate (Chokushimon) repurposed from that former residence. The gate was originally constructed in the first year of Tenmei (1781 AD) in a three-bay structure with two bays between the beams, single-storied, in the kirizuma style with a thatched roof and side enclosures (designated as a Chiba Prefecture Cultural Property). Also, the Kōunkaku located to the northeast was built in 1896 (Meiji 29) and is registered as a Registered Tangible Cultural Property.

=== Sacred Keystone (Kanameishi) ===
[[File:Katori-jingu kanameishi.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Shrine for the Sacred Keystone}}]]
[[File:Kaname-ishi-stone,katori-jingu,katori-city.japan.JPG|thumb|150px|right|{{Center|Shape of the Sacred Keystone}}]]
The '''Sacred Keystone''' (Kanameishi) is a sacred stone located to the west within the shrine grounds. Its shape is convex.
In ancient times, earthquakes were believed to be caused by a giant catfish (Ōnamazu) dwelling beneath the earth; the Sacred Keystone is said to serve as a talisman that restrains this catfish and thus protects against earthquakes. In both Kashima and Katori Jingu the keystone is described as a peg that holds down the head and tail of the giant catfish—though it appears small on the surface, its portion underground is substantial and is said to be impossible to remove. According to tradition, when Tokugawa Mitsukuni visited the shrine in the first year of the Jōkyō era (1684 AD), he ordered an excavation around the keystone, but the dig did not reach its base.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=63}}</ref> (Note: Kashima Jingū features a concave keystone with a similar legend.)
=== Other Sacred Objects and Notable Items ===
[[File:Katori-jingu sannotorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Third Torii}}]]
[[File:練習艦かとりの錨.jpg|thumb|right|{{Center|Anchor of the Katori Training Ship}}]]
* Sacred Tree – A giant cedar in front of the worship hall, reputed to be about 1,000 years old.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=52}}</ref>
* “Scout Cedar” – A cedar reputed to have been climbed by a scout dispatched by Minamoto no Yoriyoshi (no longer extant).<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=52}}</ref>
* “Three-branched Cedar” – A cedar said to have split into three branches in response to Minamoto no Yoriyoshi’s prayer (one of which has since withered). According to legend, Yoriyoshi prayed to this cedar for peace throughout the land, the prosperity of the shrine’s head, and the longevity of his descendants.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=52}}</ref>
* “Komomo Cedar” – Located to the left of the Roof Gate. Tokugawa Mitsukuni reportedly named it in the first year of the Jōkyō era (1684 AD), considering it the “mother” of the many cedars on the shrine grounds (it has since withered).<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=50}}</ref>
* “Kimon Sakura” – A cherry tree said to have been hand-planted by Tokugawa Mitsukuni during his visit in 1684; the tree now stands as the sprout grown from that original seedling.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=51}}</ref>
* “Taishō Tennō Hand-Planted Pine” – A pine that was planted by Emperor Taishō when he was Crown Prince in the 44th year of the Meiji era (1911 AD).<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=51}}</ref>
* “Hitachi-no-Miya Hand-Planted Pine” – A pine planted by Prince Hitachi-no-Miya on April 7, Showa 41 (1966 AD).<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=53}}</ref>
* The anchor of the training ship [[Katori (training ship)|Katori]] of the {{ill|Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force|en|Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force|qid=Q731647|lt=Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force|1=Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force}}.
* The sacred pond.
* Sakura Bamboo Field – An area offering views of Mount Tsukuba, Kamegase-yama, Katori-ga-ura, and the sixteen islands of Satogai.
* The Deer Enclosure – In 2015 the shrine’s sacred deer were transferred to the Katori Deer Protection Association and are now kept on the shrine grounds.
* Amakudai (Rain-praying Mound) – Located near the Okugū. According to tradition, during a drought in the 4th year of the Jōkyō era (732 AD), a platform was erected here for praying for rain.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=62}}</ref>
== Approach (Sandō) ==
There are two approaches to the shrine, each marked by its own torii.

The Omote-sandō (main approach) extends from the center of the former city of Sawara, corresponding to Chiba Prefecture Route 55. Near the intersection with Route 56 stands the First Torii ({{Coord|35|53|15.71|N|140|30|41.09|E|region:JP-12_type:landmark|name=First Torii}}). The distance from the First Torii to the Second Torii is approximately 1.6 km along this pathway.

The other approach begins at Tsunomiya in Katori City. Its starting point is along the Tone River bank, where a seaward torii (Hama Torii) stands ({{Coord|35|54|05.82|N|140|31|34.12|E|region:JP-12_type:landmark|name=Tsunomiya Beach Torii}}). Tradition holds that the deity is said to have landed here, and this torii’s road was once the Omote-sandō.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=57}}</ref> According to the "Koyuki" of the 3rd year of the Jichō era (1023 AD)<ref group="Primary Source">''Koyuki'', Jichō 3 (1023 AD), September 6.</ref>, the Katori envoy (Tsukai) departed from Kashima Jingū and is recorded as going to “Watarai, Katori Jingu,” indicating that routine offerings from across the sea to Katori Jingu were made—as is still done today during the Shikinen Jinkō-sai when the mikoshi is loaded onto a ceremonial boat. Near this torii, remnants of the once-prosperous ferry trade remain, including the Jōya-dō (designated as a cultural property by Katori City) and a monument with a poem by Akiko Yosano.
The path from the First to the Second Torii is about 2.5 km, along which external subsidiary shrines such as Shinobi Jinja, Odajinja, and others are located.

At the end of the approach on the shrine side, the path from the Second Torii continues to the Roof Gate. In ancient times, however, the road would have turned at a right angle in front of the Roof Gate and continued westward to the Okugū.<ref name="Katori Heritage">[http://www.city.katori.lg.jp/05sightseeing/kyouiku/bunkazai/b05a.html#Vol-001 Vol-001: Katori Jingu – the Ichinomiya of Shimousa] (Katori City “Katori Heritage” website).</ref>

== Subsidiary Shrines ==
The subsidiary shrines (Sessatsu-sha) consist of 9 shrines (3 located within the shrine grounds and 6 outside) and 21 branch shrines (7 located within and 14 outside), totaling 30 shrines.<ref>According to "Shinshū Katori Jingu Shoshi", pp. 35–40.</ref>

=== Subsidiary Shrines ===
{{Coordinates List|section=Subsidiary Shrines}}
The subsidiary shrines were officially designated on March 21, 1877, by a notice from the Ministry of Home Affairs.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=37}}</ref>

Amanonamae is considered the divine offspring of Keizutsushi and the ancestral deity of the Katori clan, and is thus also known as “Wakamikami Jinja.”<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=5}}</ref> Takenu-no-mikoto is regarded as the progeny of Kashima Jingū’s deity, while Ame Oshikumo is regarded as the child of Amanokoyane. To the right of its main hall, an exposed stone chamber from an ancient tomb—known as the “Matami Kofun”—remains and has been designated a historic site by Katori City.

It is said to have been founded in the 40th year of Emperor [[Keikō]]’s reign.<ref>[http://www.city.katori.lg.jp/05sightseeing/kyouiku/bunkazai/b05i.html#Vol-085 Vol-085: Ōto Jinja] (Katori City “Katori Heritage” website).</ref> Three mirror faces (Rauryūō Men and Naso Men) and three Japanese mirrors from it have been designated as Chiba Prefecture Cultural Properties.

:* Enshrined Deity: [[Kagu-tsuchi|Kagutsuchi no Kami]] and [[Haniyasu-hime no Kami|Haniyasu-hime no Kami]]
: “Kayada Jinja” is an external subsidiary shrine, formerly a village shrine. It is said to have been founded in the 18th year of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|qid=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu|1=Emperor Jimmu}}’s reign, similar to the main shrine; ancient documents from the Kamakura period refer to it as “Kayada Akuōshinja.”<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=39}}</ref> The grounds contain stone monuments that recall the prosperous ferry trade of old.<ref name="Katori Heritage">[http://www.city.katori.lg.jp/05sightseeing/kyouiku/bunkazai/ Vol-? Katori Heritage]</ref> Its main hall is an Edo-period structure designated as a Chiba Prefecture Cultural Property.

=== Former Subsidiary Shrines (Gen-Sessatsu-sha) ===
The following five shrines, though no longer affiliated as subsidiary shrines of Katori Jingu, are attested in ancient documents.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|pp=39–40}}</ref>
* [[Kanzaki Jinja]] (located in Kanzaki Town, Katori District, Chiba Prefecture)
* Takafusa Jinja (located in Yamada, Katori City)
* Kitte Jinja (located in Ōne, Katori City)
* [[Higashi Ōja]] (located in Miyamoto, Tōshō Town, Katori District)
* [[Kiuchi Ōkami (Katori City)|Kiuchi Jinja]] (located in Kiuchi, Katori City)
== Festivals ==
=== Shikinen Jinkō-sai (Cycle Festival) ===
[[File:Jinko Festival,Tsunomiya,Katori Jingu Shrine,Katori-city,Japan.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Shikinen Jinkō-sai (2014)}}]]
Every 12 years, the grand cycle festival known as '''Shikinen Jinkō-sai''' is held in the year of the Horse. Although a smaller Jinkō-sai is held annually in front of the shrine, during the cycle festival the event is held on April 15 and 16 over two days on a grand scale. In ancient times it was also known as the “Military God Festival” or “War Formation Festival.”<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (National History)|1983}}</ref>

This festival is said to reenact the subjugation of the eastern lands by Keizutsushi.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (Heibonsha)|1996}}</ref> Originally called the “Shikinen Sengu Taikai” (Cycle Rebuilding Grand Festival), it was held in conjunction with the 20-year Shikinen Sengu, but fell into decline during the Ōnin War and ceased after the 11th year of the Ōreki era (1568 AD). It was revived in the 8th year of the Meiji era (1875 AD) and held annually until from the 15th year of Meiji (1882 AD) onward it was fixed to occur only in Horse years, a practice that continues today.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Jingu (National History)|1983}}</ref>

The sequence of the festival is as follows:<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=26}}</ref>
* On the 15th: A procession centered on a mikoshi departs from the shrine and arrives at Tsunomiya. On the Tone River bank, the mikoshi is transferred to a ceremonial boat, and a boat festival is held. Then, a welcoming ceremony is conducted by Kashima Jingū. After ascending the Tone River to the mouth of Sawara, the procession stays overnight at the travel lodge.
* On the 16th: The procession returns overland to the shrine.

[[File:Rice-transplanting Festival in Katori-jingu 1,katori-city,japan.jpg|thumb|180px|right|{{Center|Otauesai (Rice-planting Festival)}}]]
; [[Katori Jingu Otauesai|Otauesai]]
: “Otauesai” is held on the first Saturday and Sunday of April. On the first day, a plowing ceremony is performed; on the second day, a rice-planting ceremony is conducted—both are grand-scale events. The festival involves performing rice-planting in the shrine’s sacred fields to pray for a bountiful harvest. Historical records indicate that by the 2nd year of Meitoku (1391 AD) the festival was already in existence,<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=29}}</ref> and it is counted among “Japan’s Three Great Rice-planting Festivals”.<ref group="Note">“Japan’s Three Great Rice-planting Festivals” include those of Katori Jingu, [[Izazu Miya]] (located in Shima, Mie Prefecture), and [[Sumiyoshi-taisha|Sumiyoshi Taisha]] (in Osaka).</ref><ref name="Spring"/>
; Reisai and Jinkō-sai
: Held on April 14 and 15 respectively, these are both grand-scale ceremonies. Reisai is considered the most important festival of the shrine. As Katori Jingu is one of the Chokusaisha, it receives an imperial envoy in years that occur every 6 years (in the years of the Child and the Horse).<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=25}}</ref> On the day after Reisai, the Jinkō-sai is performed, during which a procession dressed in traditional Heian-era attire marches and a ceremony using a portable palace is held in the parking area.<ref name="Spring">[http://www.katori-jingu.or.jp/siki_spring.htm Spring] (Official Website).</ref>
; Daikyō-sai
: “Daikyō-sai” is held on January 30 as a medium-scale ceremony. It is said to commemorate the deities’ labor after subjugating the land.<ref>{{sfn|Katori Shoshi|1995|p=33}}</ref> After sunset, the ceremony features a variety of rare sacred offerings presented before the deities.<ref>[http://www.katori-jingu.or.jp/siki_winter.htm Autumn] (Official Website).</ref>

== Cultural Properties ==
{{Small|(Below are the cultural properties associated with Katori Jingu, excluding those of independent external subsidiary shrines.)}}
=== National Treasures ===
* One bronze mirror with grapevine motifs (Kaijū Budōkyō) (craftsman’s work)
** With a diameter of 29.6 cm, an edge height of 2 cm, and weighing 537.5 g, it is made of white copper.<ref name="Fusa"/></ref> It is a work from the Tang dynasty.
** The mirror’s back features a design with grapevine scroll patterns, upon which a lion and various birds, beasts, and insects are depicted. The name “Kaijū” refers to the depiction of a legendary creature (often identified with the Chinese [[Sangei]]) on the central knob. Although a nearly identical mirror exists in the Shōsōin’s South Warehouse, the Katori mirror is not cast from the exact same mold; however, the two are believed to be related. The precise manner in which the mirror came to be transmitted to the shrine remains unknown.<ref>See “Weekly Asahi Encyclopedia: National Treasures of Japan,” Issue 89 (Asahi Shimbun, 1998; commentary by Akio Kawajiri).</ref> It is exhibited in the treasure hall and was designated on March 31, Showa 28.
=== Important Cultural Properties (National Designation) ===
* The main hall (with one plaque and one inscription) and the roof gate (in two parts) (buildings)
** The main hall was designated on June 27, Showa 52; the roof gate was added on December 26, Showa 58.
* A pair of Ko-seito yellow glazed ceramic komainu (guardian dog statues)
** These two statues (representing the A (Ah) and Un types) are made of ceramic; the A-type stands at 17.6 cm and the Un-type at 17.9 cm.<ref name="Fusa"/></ref> Based on stylistic evidence, they date from the late Kamakura or early Muromachi period.<ref name="Fusa"/></ref> They are exhibited in the treasure hall and were designated on March 31, Showa 28. (The A-type image also appears on a 250-yen postage stamp issued on July 1, Showa 51.)
* One twin-dragon mirror (Sōryūkyō) (craftsman’s work)
** With a diameter of 20.5 cm and an edge height of 5 mm (in a kamaboko shape), it is made of white copper. It bears an inscription dating from the 5th year of the {{ill|Kyūan|en|Kyūan|qid=Q1193860|lt=Kyūan|1=Kyūan}} era (1149 AD) and is regarded as the oldest extant Japanese mirror with an inscription. Its decorative style is considered atypical for a Japanese mirror and appears influenced by Song dynasty Chinese or Goryeo Korean mirrors.<ref>See “Annotated Edition of New Designated Important Cultural Properties 4: Crafts I”, Mainichi Shimbun, 1981, p.260.</ref> It is exhibited in the treasure hall and was designated on November 14, Showa 28.
* Katori Ōnegi Family Documents – 15 volumes in 7 sets (381 documents) (ancient texts)
** These documents, transmitted within the Katori family (who traditionally held the position of one-negi), date from the late Heian period through the Edo period (a total of 381 documents) and have been compiled into 15 volumes across 7 sets.<ref name="Fusa"/></ref> They are considered representative regional shrine documents in the Kantō area.<ref name="Fusa"/></ref> They are privately owned and were designated on June 6, Showa 60.
=== Registered Tangible Cultural Properties (National Registration) ===
* Kōunkaku (a building) – registered on February 15, Heisei 12.
* The Worship Hall, Offering Hall, and Sacred Kitchen (collectively as one structure) – registered on April 24, Heisei 13.
=== Chiba Prefecture–Designated Cultural Properties ===
* Tangible Cultural Properties
*** Former Worship Hall (one structure, with four plaques) – designated on March 16, Heisei 19.
*** Chokushi Gate (a building) – designated on March 8, Reiwa 4.<ref name="Education Board">{{Cite web|url=https://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/seihou/kenpou/documents/r040308-13716.pdf|title=Chiba Prefecture Announcement No.2 (Reiwa 4 March 8)|publisher=Chiba Prefectural Board of Education|date=2022-02-10|accessdate=2022-02-12}}</ref>
*** A collection of ancient sacred treasures (crafts)
***: This group encompasses sacred treasures passed down at the shrine from the Nara to Edo periods—including 39 copper mirrors, two iron artifacts known as “Shindai Tate,” one iron cauldron, two gold-bronze fan-shaped divine images, six gold-bronze fans, nine bronze offering vessels (bowl-shaped), ten iron offering vessels (with legs), one tachi inscribed “Kagenarutaka,” one artifact from Genwa 4, three sets of hand-held items, 108 combs, three wooden lion mask surfaces, and one wooden inscription plaque (purportedly penned by Emperor Kameyama).<ref name="Fusa"/></ref> These are exhibited in the treasure hall and were designated on February 23, Showa 35.
* Natural Monuments
*** The forest of Katori Jingu – designated on March 19, Showa 49.

It enshrines Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi together with Shiotsuchi-no-Oji.}}]]
Because Katori Jingu once served as a base for the development of the eastern provinces, its descendant deities – that is, the [[Mikogami]] – were established in various regions. In the ''Hitachikuni Fudoki''<ref group="原" name="行方郡"/> there is already a record of branch shrines in [[Namegata District (Ibaraki)|Namegata District]].

In the ''Engishiki'' [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Jinmyōchō]] under the entry for Mutsu Province, two shrines bearing the name “Katori” are recorded as follows:
